title: The Iliad
author: Homer
openingText: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another. And which of the gods was it that set them on to quarrel? It was the son of Jove and Leto; for he was angry with the king and sent a pestilence upon the host to plague the people, because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses his priest.
about:
The Iliad is the Greek epic of the Trojan War — but only of one slice of it, the wrath of Achilles in the war's last year. Achilles, the greatest fighter in the Greek army, is dishonored by his commander Agamemnon, who takes the captive woman Achilles had been awarded as a prize. Achilles withdraws to his tent and prays to his mother, a sea-goddess, that the Greeks will suffer for the insult. They do. Hector, the Trojan champion, drives the Greek army back to their ships. Patroclus, Achilles's closest friend, borrows his armor and goes out to fight in his place. Hector kills him. Achilles, mad with grief, returns to the field and kills Hector. The poem ends not with the victory of the Greeks or the fall of Troy — those come later, in stories told elsewhere — but with the burial of Hector, witnessed by his father Priam, who has walked alone through the Greek lines to beg for the body of his son.

Composed orally in Greek around the 8th century BCE and attributed to Homer, the Iliad is the oldest substantial work of Western literature and the foundation of everything that came after. It is roughly 15,000 lines of dactylic hexameter, divided into 24 books. It does not tell the whole war — the abduction of Helen, the wooden horse, the fall of Troy are not in it. It tells fifty-one days near the end, and the rage of one man inside them.

It is also one of the great poems of grief. The second half is mostly about the death of Patroclus and what death does to the people who survive. Achilles, who in the first book is the angriest and proudest hero in the canon, ends the poem on the floor of his tent with the father of the man he has killed, weeping with him about everything they have lost. Homer makes you understand both of them at once.

angleCards.title: The wrath of Achilles.
angleCards.text: The poem announces its subject in the first word: rage. Everything that happens — the deaths, the reversals, the grief — flows from one man's wounded pride. What does Homer want you to think about that?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the wrath of Achilles from the opening quarrel to its final exhaustion — and understand what Homer is saying about pride, honor, and the destruction they bring.

angleCards.title: Hector, not Achilles.
angleCards.text: Achilles is the hero. Hector is the one you root for. He fights not for glory but for his city, his wife, his son. Homer makes the Trojan side fully human — that is the poem's moral achievement.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Iliad through Hector's eyes — the man defending something real — and understand why Homer makes the losing side so much more sympathetic.

angleCards.title: The gods as meddling personalities.
angleCards.text: Zeus, Athena, Apollo, Aphrodite — they quarrel on Olympus while men die below. They play favorites, change outcomes, rescue their favorites from death. Homer's gods are not wise or just. They are powerful and petty.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the divine interference throughout the poem — who the gods favor, why, and what Homer reveals about fate, free will, and the relationship between humans and the divine.

angleCards.title: Honor and its cost.
angleCards.text: Every warrior in the Iliad is obsessed with kleos — glory, reputation, being remembered. It drives every decision. But Homer keeps showing you what the pursuit of honor destroys: armies, friendships, families, lives.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the logic of honor (kleos) through the poem — what drives these men, what it costs them, and whether Homer endorses or questions the heroic code he is depicting.

cast.name: Achilles
cast.description: Son of Peleus, a mortal king, and Thetis, an immortal sea-goddess. The fastest, strongest, most beautiful fighter at Troy. He has chosen to die young at Troy in exchange for eternal fame, and he knows it. His rage at being dishonored by Agamemnon sets the entire poem in motion — and the second half of the poem is about what happens to that rage when grief replaces it.

cast.name: Hector
cast.description: Eldest son of Priam, husband of Andromache, father of an infant son. The Trojans' greatest defender. He fights not for glory but because his city expects it of him, and because he loves his family and his city is what keeps them safe. The scene in which he says goodbye to his wife and son before going to face Achilles is the most quietly devastating moment in the poem.

cast.name: Agamemnon
cast.description: Commander of all the Greek forces, the king the other kings have sworn to follow. He is powerful and politically clumsy. He takes Achilles's prize because he is allowed to, not because it is wise. The arrogance of that one act in the first book triggers everything that follows. Homer does not let him off, but he does make you see the situation he was trying to manage.

cast.name: Patroclus
cast.description: Achilles's closest friend, raised in his father's house. The poem keeps him at the ships through the early books — the moral counterweight to Achilles's rage. He goes out to fight wearing Achilles's armor, hoping to frighten the Trojans into retreat, and Hector kills him. His death is the pivot on which the second half of the poem turns. Achilles never recovers.

cast.name: Priam
cast.description: The aged king of Troy, who watches from the walls as the war takes his sons one after another. In Book 24, after Achilles has killed Hector and dragged the body around the walls for days, Priam goes alone through the Greek lines, falls at Achilles's feet, kisses the hands of the man who killed his son, and asks for the body back. The scene is one of the moral high points of Western literature.

cast.name: Helen
cast.description: The most beautiful woman in the world, married to Menelaus the king of Sparta, abducted by — or run away with — Paris of Troy. Her presence in the city is the reason ten years of war have been fought around it. She appears rarely in the poem and always with a weight of guilt Homer lets her feel. She knows exactly what she has cost the people around her.

acclaim.quote: The true hero, the true subject, the center of the Iliad is force.
acclaim.context: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force, 1939

whyItMatters.title: Where the West Begins
whyItMatters.body: The Iliad is the oldest substantial work of Western literature and the soil everything else grew from. Homer's Achilles, his Hector, his Priam are characters that Plato, Virgil, Dante, Milton, Tennyson, and Joyce all wrote in conversation with. The Aeneid is a Roman rebuttal to the Iliad. Dante puts Homer in the first circle of his Inferno because he could not bring himself to put him lower. Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida is a sustained gloss on it. To read the Iliad is not to read background to Western literature — it is to start at the source. It is also a foundational treatment of grief, of pride, of the costs of taking offense. Every later work on those subjects — in epic, in tragedy, in the novel — works downstream of what Homer set down here.

whyItMatters.title: Force as the Center
whyItMatters.body: Simone Weil read the Iliad as the great poem of force — what violence does to the people who use it and the people who suffer it. The poem does not glorify war. It shows fighters becoming things, and it shows what is left of them when the fighting stops. Achilles is the most dangerous warrior in the Greek army; the poem makes you understand that being most dangerous means being least free. Hector loves his wife and his infant son and goes out to fight a war he cannot win because his city expects it of him. Priam, king of Troy, watches his sons killed one by one from the walls. Homer treats none of this as glorious. He treats all of it as the reality of force — what it costs to wield it, what it costs to suffer it, what it costs to live in a world organized around it.

whyItMatters.title: The Loss of Patroclus
whyItMatters.body: The second half of the poem is mostly grief. Achilles loses Patroclus — the man closer to him than anyone else in his life — and the rest of the poem is about that loss. He refuses to eat. He refuses to sleep. He refuses to bury the body. He goes back to the field not to win the war but to find Hector and kill him, and even after he has killed him he keeps dragging the corpse around the walls of Troy day after day. Nothing he does brings Patroclus back, and the poem refuses to let him pretend it does. The book ends only when Priam, the father of the man Achilles has killed, walks alone through the Greek lines to ask for his son's body — and the two enemies, kneeling, weep together for everything they have lost. The poem argues that war does not win against grief.
